problem_domains.problem: portfolio optimization with integer variables and hard/soft constraints
problem_domains.description: Formulating realistic portfolio optimization problems with integer holdings and both hard and soft constraints as QUBOs suitable for quantum annealing hardware.
problem_domains.quote: For the portfolio optimization problem, this mapping is particularly challenging as the DWave hardware naturally encodes problems over binary variables, but portfolio optimization is most naturally expressed with integer variables. Therefore, in addition to the overheads mentioned above, there are additional overheads in the embedding due to encoding these integer values either in binary or in unary (simpler, but with more overheads). Moreover, certain constraints in the MIP are “hard constraints” (they must be satisﬁed) while others are “soft” (merely penalized in the objective function).

solution_approaches.approach: reverse annealing
solution_approaches.description: Start from a classical solution, move to a more mixing quantum regime, then return to the original problem to escape local optima via quantum tunneling.
solution_approaches.quote: Ventuerlli and Kondratyev [VK19] described an alternative annealing approach to portfolio optimization using “reverse annealing." In this variant of annealing, one begins with a (non- optimal) classical solution to the optimization problem (say found by a classical heuristic), and then tunes the system towards a more “mixing” setting and then back again to the orig- inal problem.

solution_approaches.approach: anneal offsets
solution_approaches.description: Inhomogeneously turn on penalty terms so that some variables are driven more slowly, mitigating early freeze-out and improving annealer performance.
solution_approaches.quote: another method that has demonstrated improvements over “vanilla” quantum annealing approaches is the anneal oﬀsets approach of Adame and McMahon [AM20]. Here the idea is relatively simple. In standard quantum annealing, the penalty terms for violating a constant of the QUBO are all turned on homogeneously at the same rate. ... The basic idea behind anneal oﬀsets is to apply the penalty terms to those variables more slowly than those of the other variables.

solution_approaches.approach: amplitude amplification-based optimization

key_claims.claim: Quantum computers are expected to substantially impact finance by solving certain problems considerably faster than classical algorithms.
key_claims.quote:
Quantum computers are expected to have substantial impact on the ﬁnance
industry, as they will be able to solve certain problems considerably faster than the best
known classical algorithms.

key_claims.claim: Quantum algorithms can provide quadratic speedups for Monte Carlo methods used in derivative pricing and risk management.
key_claims.quote:
Quantum computing oﬀers a signiﬁcant speedup for Monte Carlo methods, quadratically
improving the dependence onσ and ϵ.

key_claims.claim: Out-of-the-box quantum Monte Carlo algorithms require full-scale fault-tolerant quantum computers and have very high hardware requirements.
key_claims.quote:
However, out-of-the-box implemen-
tations of such algorithms with provable guarantees all seem to require a priori full-scale
fault-tolerant quantum computing devices.

key_claims.claim: NISQ-oriented quantum finance heuristics currently lack convincing evidence of quantum speedups.
key_claims.quote:
We note that quantum solutions for ﬁnance which have been speciﬁcally designed for
NISQimplementationsdonothaveconvincingevidenceforquantumspeedups, noworinthe
long run.

key_claims.claim: Many proposed NISQ quantum heuristics in finance are heuristic without performance guarantees and may be outperformed by classical heuristics.
key_claims.quote:
First, most of these quantum algorithms areheuristic
in nature — they do not have proven performance guarantees (or if they do, they are
surpassed by classical algorithms), but neither do many classical heuristics used in practice.
It is extremely diﬃcult to compare the performance of heuristic algorithms, as oftentimes
heuristics will perform better on certain problem instances and worse on others.

key_claims.claim: Some powerful quantum algorithms for key financial challenges (Monte Carlo, portfolio optimization, machine learning) have proven asymptotic speedups.
key_claims.quote:
On the other hand, a number of powerful quantum algorithms for ﬁnance have been
proven to provide considerable asymptotic speedups over classical methods. This is true
for some of the main computational challenges in ﬁnance, including for Monte Carlo meth-
ods [Mon15], combinatorial portfolio optimization [Mon20], convex portfolio optimization
[RL18, KPS19a], and general machine learning [KP17].

key_claims.claim: Standard quantum Monte Carlo algorithms have high circuit depth and require very low error rates, limiting near-term applicability.
key_claims.quote:
As we discussed, the major limitation preventing the early commercial application of quan-
tum algorithms to Monte Carlo is thecircuit depthof the algorithm.

key_claims.claim: Current experimental implementations of quantum Monte Carlo in finance are limited to toy problems with only a handful of qubits and no advantage over classical methods.
key_claims.quote:
We emphasize that to date this algorithm has only only been performed on systems with
a handful of qubits, and has not yet demonstrated an advantage over classical methods
due to the small system sizes considered.

key_claims.claim: Quantum algorithms for convex portfolio optimization based on quantum linear system solvers are currently beyond near-term devices due to large circuit depth.
key_claims.quote:
The main limitation of these al-
gorithms is their dependence on quantum linear system solvers [HHL09, CGJ19, GSLW19]
that require large depth circuits and remain beyond the reach of near and intermediate term
devices.

key_claims.claim: Quantum machine learning algorithms often assume QRAM, which may be difficult to construct, limiting near-term applicability.
key_claims.quote:
Once more, “out-of-the-box” quantum machine learning algorithms require full
scalequantumcomputersandmoreover, assumetheavailabilityofaquantumrandomaccess
memory (QRAM), which is a quantum analogue of the classical Random Access Memory
(RAM) and may be diﬃcult to construct.

Essentially, Burchard showed that any quantum algorithm
making p parallel calls to the market modelS and bounded payoﬀ functionsf, and which
calls them at mostD times in series must have thatpD2≥ Ω(1/ϵ2)... Essentially
depth-D parallel runs of the algorithm can at most achieve aD-fold speedup over classical
Monte Carlo4.

key_claims.claim: The Kerenidis-Prakash algorithm achieves optimal speedup for a given depth and matches the Burchard bound, enabling a smooth continuum between classical and quantum Monte Carlo.
key_claims.quote:
They showed that by using carefully chosen sub-linear schedules for depth
reduction, where the depth schedules can also be selectedadaptively, one can achieve the
optimal speedup for the given depth, namely it tightly matches Burchard’s bound.

key_claims.claim: Quantum computing has the potential to considerably impact the finance sector, provably with full-scale quantum computers and possibly in the NISQ era.
key_claims.quote:
It should be clear by now that quantum computing has the potential to impact con-
siderably the ﬁnance sector, provably with the advent of full-scale quantum computers and
possibly in the NISQ era as well, both through the NISQ-iﬁcation of powerful quantum
algorithms and the better design and tuning of quantum heuristics.

key_claims.claim: Current prototype quantum computers are far from meeting the hardware parameters needed for practical Monte Carlo speedups.

key_claims.quote: The approach of Kerenidis and Prakash, while it sacriﬁces some of the quantum speedup, does successfully decrease the stringent error correction requirements of the standard algorithm. In particular, it could place the ﬁrst practical speedups for Monte Carlo — in a specialized parameter regime of relatively simple payoﬀ functions and relatively high desired accuracy ϵ — within reach of “intermediate-scale” devices capable of error rates of merely 10^−5−10^−7

key_claims.claim: Quantum linear system solvers can in some cases provide considerable speedups for unconstrained portfolio optimization compared to classical algorithms.

key_claims.quote: Again, the main limitation of the algorithm is its dependence on quantum linear system solvers [CGJ19, GSLW19] that require large depth circuits and remain beyond the reach of near and intermediate term devices.

key_claims.claim: Mixed-integer portfolio optimization is NP-complete, so no efficient classical or quantum algorithm can solve all instances under standard assumptions.
key_claims.quote: In its most general formulation, constrained portfolio optimization as described in Equation (3.2) is a mixed integer program (MIP), which is known to be NP-hard [GJ79, MS99]. Under widely believed computational assumptions, this means there is no eﬃcient classical or quantum algorithm that can solve all instances of these problems.

key_claims.claim: Existing D-Wave quantum annealers have not yet demonstrated clear quantum speedups over classical heuristic solvers.
key_claims.quote: Thus far the weight of the evidence has not supported a quantum speedup from existing hardware, though comparing the performance of heuristic algorithms vs. the DWave annealer is quite subtle

key_claims.claim: Embedding portfolio optimization into D-Wave hardware incurs significant overheads due to geometrical constraints and integer-to-binary encoding.
key_claims.quote: Together these works have provided proof of principle demonstrations that portfolio optimization problems can be mapped to existing quantum annealing hardware, albeit with signiﬁcant overheads due to a) geometrical constraints on interactions and b) the encoding of integer variables into binary variables.

key_claims.claim: Existing D-Wave portfolio optimization experiments are limited to small problem sizes despite thousands of qubits.
key_claims.quote: As a result, existing experimental implementations in D-Wave hardware have been limited in the size of the problems they can implement in hardware.

key_claims.claim: Reverse annealing can significantly improve performance over traditional quantum annealing for portfolio optimization.
key_claims.quote: They run this algorithm on with up to 60 assets on a 2048-qubit annealer, and found signiﬁcant improvements over traditional quantum annealing methods

key_claims.claim: Anneal offsets can yield orders-of-magnitude improvements in time to solution compared to standard quantum annealing.
key_claims.quote: Adame and McMahon [AM20] described a particularly simple heuristic algorithm for choosing the inhomogeneous driving schedule, and empirically showed this can provide orders of magnitude improvement in time to solution compared to standard quantum annealing, particularly on problem in- stances which the annealer found diﬃcult.

key_claims.claim: There is still substantial room to optimize quantum annealing heuristics before fair comparison with classical solvers.
key_claims.quote: This result suggests that there is still much to optimize in the implementations of these quantum annealing heuristics before comparing them to classical solvers.

key_claims.claim: It remains unknown whether near-term quantum heuristics like annealing and QAOA offer speedups over classical methods.
key_claims.quote: First, it remains open whether or not near-term amenable quantum heuristics (anneal- ing and QAOA) oﬀer a speedup over classical methods.

key_claims.claim: Careful benchmarking against best-in-class classical heuristics is required to assess practical quantum speedups in portfolio optimization.
key_claims.quote: This will require a careful comparison with best-in-class classical heuristic solvers (rather than “straw man” comparison with brute force methods, or solvers not tailored to the applica- tion), as well as with classical approximate solution methods [CW04, AMMN05, HKNP20].

key_claims.claim: Limited qubit connectivity on annealers severely restricts the size of all-to-all portfolio optimization instances that can be run.
key_claims.quote: On the annealing side, the limitation is in the quantity and con- nectivity of the qubits. The QUBO formulation of portfolio optimization usually has all to all constraints, but the limited connectivity of the existing hardware means that they can only run problem instances of much smaller sizes.

key_claims.claim: Even the largest current D-Wave annealer can only implement relatively small fully connected QUBOs compared to its physical qubit count.
key_claims.quote: For example to date the largest quantum annealer to date, the D-Wave Advantage with 5000 physical qubits, can only run all-to-all connected QUBOS on up to 180 qubits [BBRR20]

key_claims.claim: High two-qubit gate error rates limit QAOA depth and problem size, preventing its use on significant-sized portfolio optimization problems.
key_claims.quote: On the QAOA side, the quality of the qubits is the major limiting factor. Although 50+ qubit machines are already available, which could in principle be used to encode all-to-all connected 50+ qubit optimization problems (by swapping qubits), their high two-qubit gate error rates prevent this from being a viable strategy.

key_claims.claim: Much more progress in hardware is needed before production-scale portfolio optimization problems can be implemented on quantum devices.
key_claims.quote: It is clear, however, that much more progress is needed in hardware (both number of qubits, connectivity, and error rates) before production-scale problems can be implemented in quantum hardware, and the question of empirical/heuristic speedups can be evaluated.

key_claims.claim: No end-to-end quantum machine learning application with exponential speedup over classical ML is currently known.
key_claims.quote: At the present time, no end-to-end application of quantum machine learning that achieves an exponential speedup over a classical machine learning algorithm is known, and several promising candidates for such speedups had to be reconsidered [Tan19].

key_claims.claim: Quantum machine learning can still offer large polynomial speedups that are relevant for financial use cases.
key_claims.quote: However, quantum machine learning remains a promising research area as large polynomial speedups over classical ML algorithms are relevant for many use cases, including those that arise in mathematical ﬁnance.

key_claims.claim: Quantum k-NN regression can achieve a quadratic speedup in distance estimation compared to classical methods.
key_claims.quote: Quantum k-nearest neighbor regression algorithms are more promising for nearer term applications as there are eﬃcient quantum sub-routines for distance estimation and one can achieve a quadratic speedup compared to classical distance estimation.

key_claims.claim: Quantum SVM algorithms for ℓ1 penalties achieve polynomial speedups but require high-depth circuits, making them unsuitable for near-term devices.
key_claims.quote: Experimental results indicate that the quantum algorithm achieves a polynomial speedup for the ℓ1-SVM, however the algorithm uses high depth quantum linear algebra sub-routines and is therefore not suitable for near term devices.

key_claims.claim: The q-means algorithm offers polylogarithmic runtime in dataset size with guarantees comparable to robust k-means.
key_claims.quote: A quantum version q-means with the same guarantees as a robust version of the classical k-means algorithm and running time that is poly-logarithmic in data-set size has been proposed recently [KLLP19].

key_claims.claim: Finding the first impactful quantum finance applications remains a challenge but is becoming more realistic as algorithms and hardware improve.
key_claims.quote: Finding the ﬁrst quantum ﬁnance applications remains a challenge but advances in quantum algorithms to- gether with better quantum hardware continue to bring these applications closer to reality.
